findings.title: Negative queryset slicing will raise AssertionError in Django
findings.body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset is negative, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset = cursor.offset (negative). Django QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') when the start of a slice is negative (django/db/models/query.py). The in-code comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is therefore false. Because Cursor.from_string parses `int(bits[1])` without clamping, and the endpoint gates this branch on superuser/global-access + the query param `optimized_pagination=true`, any such user can craft a cursor with a negative offset and crash the audit log endpoint with a 500 (AssertionError, not a BadPaginationError). The intended 'high-performance bidirectional pagination' feature is unreachable in any working form.

findings.title: Comment falsely asserts permissions are checked for negative offsets
findings.body: The comment 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' next to the negative-offset branch implies that negative slicing is gated by some access control. No such check exists: the only gate is `self.enable_advanced_features`, which is set from the endpoint for any superuser or member with `org:global_access`. The endpoint's permission_classes (OrganizationAuditPermission) and the query filter on `organization_id` already apply to both code paths identically, so the claim is both misleading and irrelevant to the new behavior. A reviewer relying on this comment to evaluate risk would be misled about the actual attack surface.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator logic
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is an almost-verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result (lines 136-215), differing only in the extra branch that allows a negative start_offset. This duplication means any future fix, security patch, or bug fix applied to BasePaginator.get_result will silently not apply to the new paginator. Given the new class is only ever selected from one endpoint and one branch, the simpler and safer design is to add an `enable_advanced_features` flag on BasePaginator (or a small subclass that only overrides the slicing step), rather than copy the full state machine including cursor building, prev-page filtering, and post_query_filter handling.

findings.title: 'Performance optimization' comment describes a no-op change
findings.body: The diff replaces `stop = offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset; stop = start_offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. For any non-negative offset (the normal case) `max(0, offset) == offset`, so this is functionally identical to the prior code; the comment 'For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning' therefore misrepresents a no-op as a performance optimization. For prev cursors with a negative offset the behavior is also unchanged (still crashes in Django; see the related critical finding). Either remove the misleading comment or implement the actual optimization.

findings.title: Comment suggests new behavior that the code does not add
findings.body: The Cursor.__init__ change is comment-only: `self.offset = int(offset)` already accepted negative integers before this PR. The new comment 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios. This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets' implies the constructor was modified to permit this, but `int(offset)` was unchanged. This is misleading documentation in a security-sensitive area; reviewers and future maintainers may infer that negative offsets are officially supported when in fact the only consumer (OptimizedCursorPaginator) is broken and no other cursor parsing path validates bounds.

findings.title: 'authorized administrators' mislabels org:global_access
findings.body: The variable is named `enable_advanced` and the comment says 'for authorized administrators', but the condition is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `has_global_access` corresponds to the `org:global_access` scope, which is granted to Sentry employees (staff) for cross-org support, not to organization administrators. Conflating the two is a documentation/UX defect: org owners/admins will not see this code path even if they set `optimized_pagination=true`, while Sentry staff can. The branch's purpose should be described accurately (e.g. 'enable for Sentry staff and superusers') and, if intended for staff, the flag should probably not be exposed at all to non-staff.

findings.title: New query parameter and paginator branch have no tests
findings.body: The diff introduces a new query parameter `optimized_pagination`, a new permission-derived branch, and a new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator) with non-trivial behavior (negative offsets, a duplicate state machine, and a feature flag). The PR does not modify or add any tests in the diff (no files under tests/ are listed). At minimum there should be tests covering: (1) the endpoint dispatches to OptimizedCursorPaginator only when both the flag and the permission gate are set; (2) the standard DateTimePaginator path is used otherwise; (3) cursor encoding/decoding round-trips for the new path; (4) the failure mode for negative offsets (which currently is an uncaught AssertionError, see critical finding). Without tests, the 'Test 1' description and the silent code duplication are the only signals of correctness.
